How Do UN Speeches Reflect Global Priorities and Political Sentiment?

Text Analysis Project Showcase · November 3, 2026

Author

Ali Abdulmalek · POLS 4130 · Fall 2026

Research Question

What themes appear most frequently in United Nations General Debate speeches from 2004 to 2015, and how does sentiment vary across these themes?

Data

The project examines the United Nations General Debate corpus covering 2004–2015.

  • Original dataset: 5,175 records
  • Documents retained after removing unusable text: 3,149
  • Topic-modeling documents: 2,297
  • Unit of analysis: an individual text record

The analysis combines word frequency, dictionary-based sentiment, and topic modeling to investigate recurring patterns in UN speeches.

Methods

Word Frequency

Speeches were divided into individual words. Common English stopwords and nonalphabetic tokens were removed for the updated frequency chart and word cloud.

Both visualizations use the same cleaned word counts.

Sentiment Analysis

The Bing Liu dictionary assigns positive words +1 and negative words -1.

Document sentiment was calculated by summing matched dictionary values.

A separate analysis compared basic sentiment with a simple two-word negation adjustment.

Target sentiment examined dictionary words within four words of security and development.

Topic Modeling

A three-topic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model was fitted using the VEM method.

The reduced document-term matrix included:

  • 2,297 documents
  • 10,770 unique terms
  • Word-document combinations occurring at least twice

Topics were interpreted using their most probable words. Topic labels remain provisional because several words overlap.

Key Limitations

Sentiment: Dictionary scores may miss sarcasm, diplomatic context, quotations, and complicated negation. Longer speeches may accumulate larger scores.

Topic modeling: Filtering excludes some documents and words. Similar terms appear across topics, making precise labels difficult.

Interpretation: These methods measure patterns in language, not countries’ actual policy positions.

Word Frequency

Frequently occurring words reflect recurring international concerns and institutional language.

Word Cloud

The word cloud displays frequently occurring words using the same cleaned word-frequency data as the bar chart.

Sentiment Findings

Basic vs. Negation-Adjusted

The overall scores are very similar. The simple negation adjustment has little effect on the aggregate result, although individual passages may still be misclassified.

Target Sentiment

Development has a higher average dictionary sentiment than security.

This reflects nearby language rather than approval or disapproval of either issue.

Topic Modeling Findings

The model identifies three recurring themes.

Topic 1: Security and Development

Keywords: development, nations, united, international, security, global.

Topic 2: Peace and Cooperation

Keywords: nations, united, international, world, peace, people.

Topic 3: Global Development

Keywords: development, nations, united, international, countries, world.

These topic labels are interpretations of the model’s word distributions rather than predefined categories.

Top Words by Topic

Topic Proportions

Security and Development has the largest estimated average share, approximately 45%.

These figures represent estimated topic proportions, not exclusive document counts.

Sentiment by Topic

Security and Development has the highest average net dictionary sentiment score among the three topic groups.

Example Documents

The model identified the following high-weight examples:

Topic Document Evidence from the Speech
Security and Development Solomon Islands, 2015 (ID 3109) Discusses peace, security, and international cooperation.
Peace and Cooperation Document 2093 (country and year unavailable) Discusses nations working together peacefully to resolve disputes.
Global Development Mexico, 2012 (ID 1829) Discusses international cooperation, peace, and security.

These original passages provide examples of recurring UN themes. However, the speeches overlap in their language, so they do not establish completely distinct topic categories.

Interpretation and Conclusion

The analysis shows recurring language concerning development, international cooperation, security, and peace in UN General Debate texts from 2004–2015.

The word-frequency and topic-modeling results highlight related themes, although the topic labels overlap. Sentiment analysis suggests generally positive net dictionary scores, with higher average sentiment around development than security. Security and Development also has the highest average net sentiment among the three modeled topic groups.

Combining these methods provides multiple perspectives on the speeches. However, dictionary scores and topic proportions identify patterns in wording rather than directly measuring government positions or policy commitments.

Sources: United Nations General Debate corpus, 2004–2015, supplied project dataset; Bing Liu sentiment dictionary, supplied project dictionary.

Software: R, tidytext, dplyr, ggplot2, topicmodels, Quarto.
